title: Passive Devices
intro: Resistors and capacitors available in CMOS processes, their typical values and the imperfections that limit analog circuits (Razavi, Section 18.7.2).

blocks.text: Mainstream CMOS processes target digital logic and offer only transistors at first; an 'analog process' with good passives can follow a year or two later. Structures borrowed from a digital flow vary a lot from wafer to wafer because nobody optimized them.

items: Silicide-block poly: one extra mask keeps the silicide off part of a poly line, leaving doped poly of fifty to a few hundred ohms per square; silicided ends give low, reproducible contact resistance. Low capacitance to the substrate (about 90 aF/µm² plus 100 aF/µm fringe), quite linear, especially when long, but ±20% from wafer to wafer.

n-well: about 1 kΩ/□ but varying by tens of percent, with large capacitance to the substrate and a value that depends on the well-substrate voltage. Good where the exact value does not matter, for example a large isolating resistor in a bias network.
Metal: 30 mΩ/□ (top) to 100 mΩ/□ (lower layers), too low for most analog resistors.

blocks.text: An n-well resistor's capacitance is distributed and nonuniform; a rough model puts half of it at each end. As the voltage on it changes, the depletion region under it changes, and so does its resistance: a nonlinearity.
The figures of merit are density (capacitance per area), the bottom-plate parasitic to the substrate and linearity.

A MOSFET with source and drain tied together is the densest capacitor available, since the gate oxide is the thinnest layer; its bottom-plate (junction) parasitic is only 10 to 20%. But its capacitance swings from a small value (no channel: oxide and depletion in series) to $C_{ox}WL$ once the voltage exceeds $V_{TH}$, and it varies even in strong inversion.

blocks.alt: Capacitance against voltage for a MOS capacitor: low and flat below threshold, rising steeply around the threshold voltage to a flat level equal to Cox times WL. A dashed horizontal line marks a linear metal capacitor of lower value.
blocks.caption: A MOS capacitor is dense but voltage-dependent.

blocks.text: In a switched-capacitor gain stage, a nonlinear sampling capacitor transfers charge $\int C\,dV$ rather than $CV$, so the output is distorted: $V_{out} \approx V_{in} + \frac{1}{C_2}\int_0^{V_{in}}C_1\,dV$.

blocks.text: Short channels keep $\tau$ small: build MOS capacitors from many wide, short fingers rather than a square block (at the cost of more junction capacitance and area). A rule of thumb asks for $R_S < 0.1/(C\omega)$, a Q above 10.

Stacks of metal (and poly) layers give linear capacitors. Inter-metal dielectrics are thick, so density is modest, and the bottom-plate parasitic is 5 to 10% of the main capacitance. The layout chapter compares the options.

AC-coupling a stage with input capacitance $C_{in}$ through $C_C$ attenuates by $C_C/(C_C + C_{in})$, and the bottom-plate parasitic $C_P$ of $C_C$ must be put on the driving side; on the amplifier side it adds directly to the divider and can make the target attenuation impossible.

blocks.title: Coupling capacitor
blocks.text: A stage with $C_{in} = 100\text{ fF}$ is AC-coupled from a driver with $R_{out} = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, allowing 10% signal loss. $C_P = 0.1C_C$. (a) Find $C_C$ and the time constant with $C_P$ at the driver. (b) What $C_C$ is needed with $C_P$ at the amplifier?
solution: (a) $C_C/(C_C + C_{in}) \ge 0.9$ gives $C_C \ge 9C_{in} = 900\text{ fF}$. The driver sees $C_P + C_CC_{in}/(C_C + C_{in}) = 90 + 90 = 180\text{ fF}$: $\tau = 180\text{ ps}$, against 100 ps without the coupling capacitor.
(b) $C_C/(1.1C_C + C_{in}) \ge 0.9$ gives $0.01C_C \ge 0.9C_{in}$, so $C_C \ge 90C_{in} = 9\text{ pF}$: impractical. Put the bottom plate on the driver side.

blocks.title: MOS capacitor quality
blocks.text: A MOS capacitor finger has $L = 1\ \mu\text{m}$, $\mu = 400\text{ cm}^2/\text{V·s}$ and $V_{ov} = 0.5\text{ V}$. Find $\tau$ from the simple formula and its Q at 1 GHz. What if $L$ were 4 µm?
solution: $\tau = (10^{-6})^2/(4 \times 0.04 \times 0.5) = 12.5\text{ ps}$ (about 4 ps with the distributed correction).
$\tau \propto L^2$: at 4 µm it is 16 times larger and $Q \approx 0.8$, useless at 1 GHz.

blocks.title: Choosing a resistor
blocks.text: You need a 20 kΩ resistor whose value is not critical (it only isolates a bias node) and a 2 kΩ resistor that must match a reference within 1% and be linear. Which structures?
solution: 20 kΩ, value uncritical: an n-well resistor, about 20 squares at 1 kΩ/□, small area despite its ±tens of percent spread and parasitics.
2 kΩ precise: silicide-block poly (e.g. 10 squares at 200 Ω/□), laid out as matched units next to the reference.
blocks.answer: n-well for the 20 kΩ; silicide-block poly for the 2 kΩ.
